newsitem.title: USA: First trial date in Oklahoma City bombing is set.
newsitem.headline: First trial date in Oklahoma City bombing is set.

text.p: Timothy McVeigh will go on trial on March 31 for the bombing of the federal building in Oklahoma City that killed 168 people, less than a month before the blast's second anniversary, officials said on Friday.
"We can confirm that date," said James Manspeaker, spokesman for the trial judge.
McVeigh and co-defendant Terry Nichols will be tried separately for the April 19, 1995, bombing. No date has been set yet for Nichols' trial.

"We thought it was important to start before the second anniversary," Patrick Ryan, U.S. Attorney for Oklahoma, told reporters as he returned to the courthouse for a closed-door hearing on other scheduling matters.
Ryan said he expected jury selection to take about two weeks and the entire trial about two to three months.

McVeigh's attorney, Stephen Jones, declined to answer directly whether the judge will sequester the jury but did say he had not wanted the jury sequestered and would be "pleased" when the judge's order is formally entered.

Jones said he wants the jurors to maintain as normal a life as possible. "I want the jury to go home and sleep in their own beds at night and to the maximum extent possible I want the jury to lead normal lives," Jones said.

Jones said it was "too early to tell" if McVeigh will take the stand. "Certainly, he wants to and certainly I want him to. But until we know all of the evidence it's hard to know if it will be necessary for Mr. McVeigh to testify," Jones said.
Lead prosecutor Joseph Hartzler said U.S. District Court Judge Richard Matsch imposed the date after the two sides failed to reach an accord.
On Thursday, Jones said he did not believe he could be ready before May 1. Prosecutors have maintained all along that they are ready to go to trial.
But when Jones was asked on Friday if he was happy about the date, he said, "you bet."
The case has been moved to Denver because it was deemed nearly impossible for the two men to receive a fair hearing anywhere in Oklahoma.
Victims and relatives of people who perished in the bombing have wanted the trial to begin as soon as possible. Some of them have attended all the pre-trial hearings.

One relative, Marsha Kight, had a mixed reaction. "It brings some anxiety, but it feels good, too. It's really going to happen. I guess I'm ready," said Kight, whose daughter, Frankie Merrell, died in the bombing.
This week's hearings have focused on how much information prosecutors must turn over to the defence.
Prosecutors are obliged to provide defendants evidence they will or might use in a trial. They must also hand over any information in their possession that might help the defence side.
In the open court part of Friday's session Jones questioned whether a key prosecution witness changed his story as part of deal to avoid trial.
"He's come 180 degrees," Jones said in reference to Michael Fortier, a former associate of McVeigh's who has agreed to testify for the government in exchange for a plea agreement.
Jones has been provided with Fortier's grand jury testimony and other documents. He wanted details on negotiations between Fortier and authorities, which he described as "horsetrading."
Hartzler said there was "no dickering back and forth" and no written statements on any such meetings. The judge accepted Hartzler's argument.
